title: Real-Life Budget Challenge
tagline: Real prices · A buffer · A day you actually do
goal: Your kid plans a day out the family will actually do, inside a real budget: a beach day, a birthday outing, a day trip. They find the real prices, build in a buffer, pitch it to you, then run the money on the day and see how close they came. It's the maths every adult uses: can I afford this, and what do I cut when I can't?
need: A day out you're willing to do in the next few weeks, and a budget for it
Paper and a pencil, or a notes app, and a calculator
A phone or computer to find real prices
On the day: the cash, or a card and the job of tracking every spend

lesson.text: A budget is a plan that has to add up. When it doesn't, you don't change the budget: you choose what to cut, and say why.
lesson.before: We'll go to the beach and get lunch and stuff.

model.line: $100 for a family beach day for 4.
Gas $15, lunch 4 × $9 = $36, kayak 2 hours × $15 = $30, ice cream 4 × $6 = $24.
Bring snacks from home ($8) instead of ice cream. New total: $89, with $11 left for surprises.

lesson.modelNote: 'And stuff' hides the money. With every item priced, the $5 over shows up right away, and one swap fixes it.

howTo.intro: Let the first plan blow the budget. That's where the good part starts. They pick the scenario and every price, and your main line is 'what would you cut?', asked far more often than 'what's the answer?'

plan.what: Pick the day, find the real prices and build the plan (Steps 1 to 3).
Pitch it and survive the what-ifs (Step 4).
Run the money, then total it up at home (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Good. The website, the menu or the phone call in Step 2 will fix it, and the surprise is the lesson.

troubleshoot.q: We can't do a big day this month
troubleshoot.a: Do a small real one: a $20 park-and-treat afternoon uses the same five steps. Keep the big plan for later.

steps.title: Pick a real day and set the budget
steps.why: A day your kid wants, a number it has to fit inside, and a promise: if it fits, you go.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a day out the family will really do in the next few weeks: a beach day, a birthday outing, a day trip, a movie and dinner. You set the budget together, and they write it at the top of the page: 'Our day is ___ on ___, and the budget is $___.'
steps.you: Pick a budget you'd truly spend, and say the deal out loud: if the plan fits, we do it. Rough guides: a simple day out $50 to $75, a bigger outing $100 to $150, a day trip $150 to $200.
ask: What day would be really fun to plan?
How much do you think a day like that costs?
steps.tip: A day they can't wait for makes every number matter. Kids who've never handled money misjudge prices wildly, so let them find out.

levels.explore: Pick a small day, like the park and a treat, with $20 to $40 in cash you can hold.
levels.develop: Pick a bigger day and explain why the budget makes sense for it.
levels.extend: Say the family has $300 a month for fun. What share should this day get, and what does that leave for other weekends?

steps.title: Find the real prices
steps.why: Not guesses: what it actually costs, and where that number came from.
steps.kid: Your kid lists everything the day will cost, from getting there to the last treat, and finds the real price of each: the place's website, a menu online, last time's receipt or a phone call. They write how many, the price each and where it came from. The Hidden costs card in the Day Out Toolkit at the end of the guide catches the ones everyone forgets.
steps.you: Help with the phone call or the website if they need it, then let them write it down. Don't point out a missing cost yet. The day itself will.
ask: What will you actually spend money on?
Where did that price come from?
steps.tip: Restaurant prices don't include tax or a tip. Adding about a quarter on top keeps the bill from surprising anyone.

levels.explore: Find real prices for 3 or 4 things with a grown-up, and write each one down.
levels.develop: Price every item, and note where each price came from.
levels.extend: For 2 items, find 3 prices each. Plan with the middle one, not the cheapest, and say why.

steps.title: Build the plan, the buffer and a cut list
steps.why: Does it fit with room to spare? If not, what goes?
steps.kid: Your kid writes each item, how many, the price each and the line total, then adds a grand total, like the beach day example. Then they hold back a buffer for surprises, about 10% of the budget, and rank a cut list: what goes first if the day costs more. Over budget? They cut now, and say why.
steps.you: Let them struggle with it before you jump in. 'I want bowling and the arcade, but I can only afford one' is the best lesson in the guide.
ask: What's your grand total, and how much is in the buffer?
What's first on your cut list, and why?
steps.tip: Use the Buffer and cut list card: a $100 budget means $10 held back, so the plan has to fit in $90.

levels.explore: Add up the plan on a calculator, then hold back $5 for surprises.
levels.develop: Build the full plan with a 10% buffer and a cut list of 3 things.
levels.extend: Find each category's share of the budget, set a rule like 'nothing over 40%', and check the plan passes.

steps.title: Pitch it and survive the what-ifs
steps.why: A plan is only ready when it holds up to a surprise.
steps.kid: Your kid pitches the day to you: what it costs, what's in the buffer and why it's worth it. You throw two what-ifs at it: parking is $8, it rains, gas went up $6, one place is closed. For each one, they show where the money comes from, using the buffer or the cut list. If the plan holds, you approve it and pick the date.
steps.you: Listen like you're really deciding, because you are. Don't offer more money. If a what-if breaks the plan, send it back for one fix, not a rebuild.
ask: Where does the money for that come from?
What would make you cut the activity instead of the snacks?
steps.tip: Kids who built a buffer in Step 3 suddenly understand why adults do. Kids who didn't usually add one now, on their own.

levels.explore: Tell the plan out loud and handle one what-if with the buffer.
levels.develop: Pitch with the numbers, handle two what-ifs, and fix the plan if one breaks it.
levels.extend: Work out the cost per hour of fun for each activity, and use it to defend your priciest choice.

steps.title: Do the day and track it
steps.why: The real day is the test. The receipts are the results.
steps.kid: On the day, your kid carries the plan and keeps score with the Day tracker card: each time money is spent, they write the planned price, the real one and the difference. When something costs more, they decide on the spot: buffer first, then the cut list. At home, they total it up. Over or under, and which line was furthest off?
steps.you: Hand them the cash, or the job of tracking every spend, and let them make the calls, even ones you'd make differently. Save your opinions for the drive home.
ask: Which line was furthest off, and why?
What will you plan differently next time?
steps.tip: 'We planned $36 for lunch and spent $44' sticks in a way no practice plan does. Write what they'd change at the top of the plan, for next time.

levels.explore: Hold the cash for one part of the day, like lunch, and count what's left.
levels.develop: Track every spend against the plan and handle a real surprise with the buffer or the cut list.
levels.extend: Work out how far off each category was as a percentage, and write two rules for planning the next day out.

after.label: Budget maths
lines: Line total = how many × price each

conclusion.headline: Every dollar has a job.
conclusion.text: Lay their plan next to the receipts and find the line that was furthest off. Ask why, and listen: 'I forgot tax' or 'we stayed longer' is exactly what they'll catch before it happens next time.
conclusion.celebrate: When they cover a surprise on the day without asking for more, say: 'You found that money inside your own plan. I'd have reached for my wallet.'
extensions: Plan the same day with half the money
Run a second day using the two rules they wrote
Give them a small monthly fun budget to manage
Plan a family trip where everyone gets one must-have category

signs: They ask how much things cost before planning
They leave a little extra for surprises
They say 'we can do this if we skip that'
makeItReal: Give them a small monthly fun budget of their own, and let them plan how it gets spent, one outing at a time.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: When we planned three days at Universal Studios, my son did the budget with me. He hunted for the best ticket prices, compared hotels, and looked up what the restaurants actually charge. He estimated about $3,000 Canadian. When we added up what we really spent, it came to $3,400.
